stem: Box A contains 3 cards numbered 1, 2 and 3. Box B contains 2 cards numbered 1 and 2. One card is removed at random from each box, and the grid shows every possible pair of cards. Tap every outcome in the event "the product of the two numbers is at least 3".
solution: The sample space is every pair (card from Box A, card from Box B): $3 \times 2 = 6$ outcomes, namely $(1, 1)$, $(1, 2)$, $(2, 1)$, $(2, 2)$, $(3, 1)$ and $(3, 2)$.
"At least 3" means 3 or more, so a product of exactly 3 is included.
Work out each product in turn: $1$, $2$, $2$, $4$, $3$, $6$.
The products that are 3 or more come from $(2, 2)$, $(3, 1)$ and $(3, 2)$. Tap those three cells.
The event set is $E = \{(2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2)\}$, with $n(E) = 3$ out of $n(S) = 6$, which is where the book's answer $P(E) = \frac{1}{2}$ comes from.
notes: From the book's end-of-chapter two-box question (ex14-8-22c, answer 1/2). A non-square 3 x 2 grid and an inequality rule (at least 3) take the same skill, finding every outcome that gives the wanted result, off the two-dice picture. The common slip is reading "at least 3" as "more than 3" and so dropping (3,1); that fires missed-outcomes, mapped to event-set-incomplete. extra-outcomes (tapping a product of 2) has no own misconception on this objective, so it is deliberately unmapped. counted-once is also left unmapped: no two cells of the event share a product (4, 3, 6), so it cannot be the likely signal here. The product rule is symmetric in the two boxes, so which axis the grid draws Box A on does not change the question.
